episodes.about: For decades, the idea of AI improving itself was just a thought experiment. Today, AI is already helping researchers at frontier labs run experiments, write code and test ideas faster. Mark Chen says OpenAI has built “AI research interns.” So how far are we from AI that can do the research on its own? In the first episode of Working Theory, a16z general partner Sarah Wang explores recursive self-improvement with Mark Chen, Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, and John Schulman, co-founder and Chief Scientist of Thinking Machines Lab and co-founder of OpenAI. They cover what RSI actually means, why research taste is so hard to teach, and why AI may be one of our best tools for solving alignment.
episodes.title: Can AI Learn to Improve Itself? | Recursive Self-Improvement
episodes.why: OpenAI research chief Mark Chen and Thinking Machines co-founder John Schulman on recursive self-improvement — Chen says OpenAI has built 'AI research interns,' and they get into why research taste is the hard part to teach.

episodes.about: Patrick Gray and James Wilson are joined by special guest co-host Jason Kikta, CISO at METR.org, to talk through the week's cybersecurity news. The headline material draws on Google's GTIG AI Threat Tracker — agentic threat activity crosses a significant threshold — including what Google says was the first fully automated AI cyberattack, hackers using AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks, and an FBI flash alert on a tool automating cyberattacks at machine speed. Also in the show: Optimizely confirms hackers put malicious code into customer sites, CNN and BBC readers got malware with their daily news, and Nightmare Eclipse has dropped so many Windows 0-days that it's getting boring.
episodes.title: Risky Business #860 -- Google: Agentic hacking has “crossed a threshold”
episodes.why: Discovery pick — Risky Business is a long-running Australian cybersecurity news show; with METR's CISO Jason Kikta guest-hosting, it works through Google's finding that agentic hacking has crossed a threshold, including a fully automated AI cyberattack.

episodes.about: After years of unexplained and severe symptoms, WSJ reporter Katie Bindley turned to AI, handing her extensive medical history to Google Gemini. She walks us through how the tool helped her uncover a diagnosis doctors overlooked, and the potential of AI to bridge gaps in healthcare. Julie Chang hosts.
episodes.title: How AI Connected Decades of Medical Clues Doctors Missed
episodes.why: WSJ reporter Katie Bindley handed Gemini her extensive medical history after years of unexplained, severe symptoms — and it connected the clues to a diagnosis her doctors had missed.

episodes.about: Ben Hein, CEO of the Electronics business at Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, joins Jon Krohn to explain how the chips behind the AI boom are actually made. His company supplies materials, systems and services across all six steps of semiconductor fabrication, a process of more than 1,500 steps that can take six months for a single chip. In this episode, he explains why performance per watt is the industry's single biggest problem, why five decades of shrinking has given way to building upward, how AI-driven simulation lifted his R&D hit rate more than fivefold, and what neuromorphic chips modeled on the 20-watt brain could change.
episodes.title: 1045: How AI Chips Are Built, with Benjamin Hein
episodes.why: Merck Electronics CEO Benjamin Hein walks through all six steps of making an AI chip — a 1,500-step process that can take six months for one chip — and why performance per watt is now the industry's biggest problem.

episodes.about: New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. This story was written by Casey Crownhart and narrated by Noa.
episodes.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
episodes.why: Discovery pick — MIT Technology Review's narrated-article feed; Casey Crownhart on solid-state transformers, a grid staple being reinvented to cut the power losses that come with the AI boom.
